questions.prompt: Walk through creating a contract from NextCRM's account page, from the submit click to the toast: how the form turns its fields into the action's input, how that input crosses to the server, what createSafeAction does with it and where its types come from, what happens when currency is left unpicked or value is "" or "12,000", and what the client does on success.

keyPoints.text: [w2] The form builds the typed input by hand from FormData. Each date comes from a hidden input holding date.toISOString(), and the picker starts at new Date(), so all five dates, both signature dates included, default to today and always parse.

[w2] execute calls the imported server action like a function, but React serializes the argument object (Date values included) into a POST to the server, so the action receives whatever body a client sends, not what the form's types promise.

[w3] createSafeAction is the real boundary: it runs safeParse against CreateNewContract and, on failure, returns { fieldErrors } from flatten() instead of throwing; on success the handler gets the parsed object, from which zod has stripped every key the schema does not name.

[w3] The types are derived, not copied: InputType is z.infer of the schema and ReturnType is ActionState<InputType, {}>, so FieldErrors has exactly the schema's keys and useAction is typed from the action it is given.

[w2] An unpicked currency submits "" from the select's hidden input, and length(3).optional() accepts undefined but not "", so the user gets a currency field error even though the handler treats a missing currency as allowed.

[w2] value is any string to the schema: "" passes zod and is caught by the handler's own check, which shows as a generic error toast rather than a field error, while "12,000" passes both and parseFloat stores 12 in a Decimal(18,2) column.

[w2] The audit row is best effort: writeAuditLog catches and logs its own failure and never rethrows, so a contract can exist without an audit entry, and a Prisma error on the create comes back as one generic error string.
[w1] On success the action returns { data: { title } }; useAction stores it and calls onSuccess, which toasts, closes the sheet and calls router.refresh(). The action itself revalidates no path.

questions.prompt: Explain the three input boundaries NextCRM's server actions use, taking createNewContract, createInvoice and updateAccount as the examples: what each lets the wire carry, what reaches Prisma, how a bad input fails, and how the client finds out. Then say what one rule would make all three safe.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Actions wrapped in createSafeAction are parsed and stripped before the handler runs, and validation failures come back as data ({ fieldErrors }) that the form renders under each input by its id.

[w3] createInvoice takes raw: unknown and calls createInvoiceSchema.parse after authentication, so its typed input exists only after parsing; a bad payload throws a ZodError, so the caller gets a rejected promise, not field errors.
[w3] updateAccount declares a 25-field TypeScript parameter and parses nothing. The annotation is erased at runtime, so whatever object arrives is what runs.

[w3] It then spreads ...rest into the Prisma data, so any real column the caller adds, such as createdBy or deletedAt, is written, and so is updatedBy, which the action sets before the spread and the caller can override; only keys that are not columns fail, inside the try, as "Failed to update account".

[w2] Each style fails differently: createSafeAction returns { fieldErrors } or { error } values, createInvoice throws Error("Unauthorized"), Error("Forbidden") or a ZodError, and updateAccount returns { error } strings, so client code needs three ways to handle errors.
[w2] The rule underneath: a TypeScript type is a promise only inside the compiled program, and a server action's argument comes from outside it.
keyPoints.quote: a type annotation is a contract only within the compiled program; at process boundaries you need a parser.

keyPoints.text: [w1] The fix: put every action behind createSafeAction or raw: unknown plus a zod parse, whose object schema strips unknown keys, and pass Prisma an explicit field list instead of a spread.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict this claim about NextCRM: "Its types flow honestly from the Prisma schema to the client components." Trace a Decimal money field, such as a contract's value or an opportunity's budget, from the create form through the database to a client component, and say what you would change.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Money columns such as value and budget are Decimal(18,2), and Prisma returns them as Decimal objects, which cannot be passed to a Client Component as they are, so server code runs serializeDecimals before handing rows down.

[w3] serializeDecimals<T>(obj: T): T turns each Decimal into a number but returns the same type, so the client still sees a Decimal type while holding a number: Decimal methods compile and fail at runtime, and number arithmetic does not compile without a cast.
[w2] It is shallow: only top-level keys are converted, so a Decimal inside an included relation stays a Decimal, which is why the contract page converts lineItems separately through an any cast.

[w2] getAllCrmData converts contracts and opportunities with serializeDecimalsList but rebuilds exchange rates by hand as { fromCurrency, toCurrency, rate: Number(...) }, a second way across the same boundary in one function.

[w2] The defensible part: AccountsView types crmData as Awaited<ReturnType<typeof getAllCrmData>>, so the prop follows the server function with no hand-written copy, though it inherits serializeDecimals' wrong Decimal type.
[w1] In the same props, data: any[] leaves the main accounts table completely unchecked, so a renamed column breaks at runtime instead of at compile time.

[w2] On the write side the money path is a free string, then a float, then a Decimal (parseFloat in createNewContract), while createInvoice computes amounts with decimal.js: one app, two money disciplines.

[w2] Verdict: indict at the server-to-client boundary. Change: a mapped type such as Serialized<T> that turns Decimal into number (or a string), applied by a deep converter, plus a zod-parsed money string on the write side instead of parseFloat.
